TT-YDEB-004.question: Who were the most prominent voices in the the Canberra bushfires debate in 2003?
TT-YDEB-004.run3_answer:
Bob Brown led the selected ranking with 245 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Robert Murray Hill recorded 189 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

David Kemp recorded 111 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Lyn Allison recorded 111 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Kelvin Thomson recorded 79 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Meg Heather Lees recorded 54 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Kerry O'Brien recorded 49 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

Ian Macdonald recorded 43 chamber speeches labelled climate-environment from 2003-01-01 to 2003-12-31.

- Simon Crean told the House on 4 February 2003 that he supported the Prime Minister's motion and detailed the scale of the fire season, including the Canberra deaths among seven nationally.

- Jenny Macklin said on 4 February 2003 that the Canberra fires cost four lives and many homes, and conveyed the House's good wishes through the member for Canberra.

- Kenneth Ticehurst on 5 March 2003 praised firefighters, police, emergency services, Defence personnel and volunteers, and sent condolences to families of those who died.

- Annette Ellis described on 5 February 2003 how Saturday, 18 January 2003 was a devastating day for Canberra, with fires driven by terrain, weather and extreme drought.

- Margaret Elizabeth Reid had a media release read into the Senate on 4 February 2003 inviting Canberrans to knit squares for patchwork rugs for those who lost homes in the 18 January bushfires.

- Nick Minchin told the Senate on 24 November 2003 that Treasury offered interest-free loans to employees directly affected by the 18 January Canberra fires, and two employees took them up.
TT-YDEB-004.run5_answer: The available records do not establish an answer to this question.

retrieved_sources.title: Annette Ellis — 2003-02-05
retrieved_sources.snippet: In beginning my contribution today, could I make the point that, whilst I am obviously going to be concentrating on the fires in Canberra of 18 January, I fully recognise and acknowledge that there have been severe fires in Queensland, Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania and Western Australia—in fact, virtually right across the continent. Saturday, 18 January 2003 was a devastating day for Canberra. Fires—begun by a lightning strike some time earlier and encouraged and fed by terrain, weather conditions and extreme drought—hit our community in a way never imagined. I was at home that day in Monash, a suburb of Tuggeranong, and my neighbours and I heard the emergency warnings and prepared our houses. At the time, we had no way of knowing the actual dimension of what was happening, except to say that the heat, the wind and the overwhelming red glow followed by darkness—virtually as dark as midnight—in the middle of the afternoon told us something terrible was happening. We were lucky because the fires did not actually reach our suburb. But the statistics I am referring to are stark. It is worth noting, in referring to those statistics, that up until this time I believe it had been 51
retrieved_sources.speaker: Annette Ellis

retrieved_sources.title: Richard Kenneth Robert Alston — HIGHER EDUCATION LEGISLATION AMENDMENT BILL 2003 — 2003-08-13
retrieved_sources.snippet: The bill provides $7.3 million in 2003 to assist the Australian National University rebuild its world class research facilities at Mt Stromlo Observatory following their devastation by the Canberra bushfires on 18 January 2003. The bushfires that swept through the Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics site destroyed heritage buildings, critical workshops and state-of-the-art telescopes that were also a key tourist attraction. The Research School has long been recognised as an important player in national and international astronomy, providing leading edge training for students as well as world class pure and applied research facilities.
retrieved_sources.speaker: Richard Kenneth Robert Alston

retrieved_sources.title: Nick Minchin — QUESTIONS ON NOTICE — 2003-11-24
retrieved_sources.snippet: (2) Following the bushfires that struck Canberra on 18 January 2003, the Treasury made an offer of assistance to employees who were directly affected by the fires - that is, through loss or substantial damage to their homes. The offer included short-term, interest free loans, based on demonstrated need. Two employees took up the offer. They were loaned $2000 and $1000 respectively. The latter has been repaid in full; the former is subject to regular repayments and will be fully paid in November.
retrieved_sources.speaker: Nick Minchin

retrieved_sources.title: Stewart McArthur — 2003-11-05
retrieved_sources.snippet: A nation charred is the result of 500 submissions from those people at the coalface of firefighting—firefighters, landowners, farmers and community people—who have been personally affected by the fires. The impact of this devastation is evidenced by the hearings that were held in Omeo, Buchan, Wodonga, Canberra and Cooma, so much so that those of us who attended those hearings were on the verge of crying when we heard about the devastation that was brought about by these fires. The fact of the matter is that four million hectares were burnt; nothing can refute that fundamental evidence. The fires burnt out about 56 years of forest production in current harvesting rates and the fires were so hot that it will mean that much of it will not recover. National parks were devastated and there is very strong evidence that this was the worst fire since 1939.The observation I make is that there was a conspiracy of silence by state authorities, bushfire brigades and the green movement, who made no comment on the fires. They were strangely silent. They said nothing for weeks and weeks about this absolute devastation. There was overwhelming evidence that fuel reduction burning is a desirable te
retrieved_sources.speaker: Stewart McArthur

retrieved_sources.title: Kate Lundy — ADJOURNMENT — 2003-02-04
retrieved_sources.snippet: A bushfire recovery appeal has been set up and is receiving strong local and outside support, with many businesses and organisations donating quite extraordinary amounts of money. About $3½ million has been collected to date. From memory, the target was $10 million for this fund. I would like to mention some of the donors to that fund. Licensed clubs throughout Canberra have rallied to the emergency by not only donating large amounts of money to the bushfire recovery appeal through ClubsACT but providing food and facilities and supporting emergency services and the efforts of other organisations. In some cases, this was as straightforward as making sandwiches on the day. In the week following the firestorm— when Belconnen and other places were still on alert; we had no idea if the fires were going to come back—those clubs made sandwiches to make sure that the volunteers, the firies and the emergency services workers had food to be able to keep going. Those little things really mattered and made a big difference.
retrieved_sources.speaker: Kate Lundy

sources.snippet: I seek leave to move the following motion: That so much of the standing orders be suspended as would prevent the private Members' business orders of the day relating to the Climate Change (National Framework for Adaptation and Mitigation) Bill 2021 and the Climate Change (National Framework for Adaptation and Mitigation) (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2021 standing in the name of the Member for Warringah being called on immediately, debated together and given priority over all other business for final determination of the House.
sources.speaker: Zali Steggall

sources.title: Zali Steggall — 2021-10-18
sources.snippet: I move: That this bill be now read a second time. This bill, the Climate Change (National Framework for Adaptation and Mitigation) (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2021, will make consequential and transitional amendments to existing acts for the purposes of the substantive bill, the Climate Change (National Framework for Adaptation and Mitigation) Bill 2021. This bill also introduces climate risk disclosure for Commonwealth entities. Commonwealth entities like government agencies and departments are exposed to the risks of climate change impacts. The Reserve Bank of Australia has observed that climate change is exposing financial institutions and the financial system more broadly to risks that will rise over time if not addressed. Since 2017, the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, TCFD, led by Michael Bloomberg, has been leading voluntary climate reporting standardisation for private companies. Companies around the world have recognised the value of climate disclosure. Benefits include more effective risk assessment, capital allocation and strategic planning. sources.title: Zali Steggall — 2020-11-09
sources.snippet: I move: That this bill be now read a second time. I've already introduced the climate change bill which puts into law, if passed, a net zero emissions target by 2050; legislates for climate risk assessment and adaptation, and resilience planning; and establishes regular technology readiness assessments and an independent climate change commission. Independent Climate Change CommissionUnderpinning the other elements of the climate change bill, is the establishment of an independent climate change commission. This body is modelled on the successful and respected Climate Change Committee in the United Kingdom. The Climate Change Committee has provided sound advice over the last decade, ensuring that the United Kingdom is on track with their Paris commitments. We have already had the Climate Change Authority, but, unfortunately, over many years of partisan attacks it has been defunded and weakened. We need a trusted independent body that the government defers to and from which the public can receive clear, independent, expert based climate advice. BL-ASNT-004.question: when did the Maritime Legislation Amendment Bill 2022 become law
BL-ASNT-004.run3_answer:
The Maritime Legislation Amendment Bill 2022 became law on 5 December 2022, when the Maritime Legislation Amendment Act 2022 received royal assent.

The bill had passed both houses on 28 November 2022, after first being introduced in the Senate on 28 September 2022.
BL-ASNT-004.run5_answer: The Maritime Legislation Amendment Bill 2022 became law as the Maritime Legislation Amendment Act 2022.
